about: Building materials (roadmap BT3a, generic stones): the common stones of the isles (sandstone, limestone, granite, marble, chalk and clunch, whinstone), Coade stone and local building stones (Magnesian Limestone, sarsen, York, Reigate, Ketton, Ancaster, Heavitree, Hopton Wood); variant links from each generic stone to the named stones of materials_stone.json. Fields as bidb/building_materials.py.

materials.name: Sandstone

period.text: Used since prehistory: the sarsens (a silicified sandstone) of Coldrum Long Barrow in Kent, where human remains were placed between 3980 and 3800 BC (-3980), are the earliest a source here names. Still quarried and built with.

regions.text: Throughout the isles: the Old and New Red Sandstones, the Carboniferous gritstones and York stone of the Pennines, the Cretaceous sandstones of the Weald

materials.technology: Easy to work for its hardness, so a common building and paving stone; some beds weather badly and have had to be replaced in old buildings.
materials.note: The more specific sandstones (red sandstones, gritstone, York stone, Reigate stone, sarsen) have entries of their own; a record that names one is linked to it, not to sandstone.

materials.name: Limestone

period.text: Used since prehistory: oolitic limestone from the Cotswolds walls the chamber of West Kennet Long Barrow, built in the 37th century BC (-3650 stands for it); the Romans and the medieval church builders used it widely. Still quarried and built with.

regions.text: Quarried and used throughout the isles: the Jurassic belt from Dorset to Yorkshire (Portland, Bath, Cotswold, Ham Hill, Barnack, Ketton, Ancaster), the Magnesian Limestone of the north-east, the Carboniferous limestone of the Pennines, Wales and most of Ireland

materials.technology: Readily available, easy to cut into blocks and to carve, and lasting, but heavy; burnt in kilns it also gave the lime of mortar and render.

materials.name: Granite

period.text: Used as found since prehistory: Brownshill dolmen, Co. Carlow, built between 4000 and 3000 BC (-3500 stands for it), has a granite capstone; Bronze Age Grimspound on Dartmoor (first settled about 1300 BC) has a granite perimeter wall. Hard to dress by hand until steam-powered cutting tools came from Aberdeen in the 19th century. Still used.

regions.text: Found in the uplands: Cornwall and Dartmoor, the Lake District (Shap), Leicestershire (Mountsorrel), Aberdeenshire and the Highlands, the Mournes, Wicklow and Galway, Guernsey and Jersey

materials.technology: Hard and durable, so long worked only as found boulders or roughly dressed; Alexander MacDonald of Aberdeen's steam-powered cutting and polishing tools (1830s) made fine dressed and polished granite possible.

examples.note: hut circles and perimeter wall of granite slabs

materials.name: Marble

period.text: Imported marble came with the Romans: Fishbourne Roman Palace, built around 75-80 AD (75), had marble polychrome panels. In the Middle Ages the 'marbles' were polished British limestones (Purbeck, later Kilkenny); white Italian marble was imported again from the 17th century, mostly for interiors and monuments. Still used.

regions.text: Almost all imported (Carrara and other Italian, Greek and French marbles); the isles' true marbles are few (Connemara, Iona, Skye); in the British sense any stone that takes a polish, as Purbeck marble

materials.note: Marble in a building is mostly for fittings (fireplaces, floors, monuments, fonts); those sentences are not counted, only columns, shafts, facings and walls. Purbeck and Kilkenny marble have entries of their own.

materials.name: Chalk and clunch

period.text: Chalk rubble was building material for the church of Hyde Abbey, Winchester, built in 1110 (with flint); clunch, the harder chalk, was cut as ashlar for walls and dressings of medieval churches in eastern England. Chalk houses still standing are mostly pre-Victorian; clunch is still quarried at Totternhoe.

regions.text: The chalk country of southern and eastern England: East Anglia (Thetford, Ely, Burwell), Bedfordshire (Totternhoe), Hertfordshire, Cambridgeshire, Surrey

materials.technology: Soft when quarried and full of water, so easily sawn, it hardens as it dries; it weathers badly unless rendered, so it was often used inside or for dressings and boundary walls.

materials.name: Whinstone

period.text: Excavation found that the 12th-century church of St Giles', Edinburgh (1101 stands for the century) was likely built of pink sandstone and grey whinstone; whinstone rubble walls are common in Scottish buildings of every later date. The word whinstone is first attested in the 16th century.

regions.text: Northern England and Scotland: the Whin Sill of Northumberland and Durham, the Pentland Hills and the Lowlands of Scotland

materials.technology: So hard that it is difficult to work and its angular pieces fit together badly; mostly laid as rubble with dressings of sandstone.

materials.name: Coade stone

period.text: Made at Eleanor Coade's Artificial Stone Manufactory in Lambeth from 1769; production ended in the early 1840s, when cast stone made with Portland cement had taken its place.

regions.text: Made in Lambeth, London, and sent all over the isles for architectural ornament, statues and garden ornaments

materials.technology: A stoneware, not a stone: a clay body cast in moulds and fired twice, virtually weatherproof; Coade perfected the recipe and the firing.

materials.name: Sarsen

period.text: Used as found since the Early Neolithic: the chamber of Coldrum Long Barrow, Kent, where human remains were placed between 3980 and 3800 BC (-3980), the other Medway megaliths and West Kennet Long Barrow (37th century BC) are of sarsen; Stonehenge's sarsen circle followed. Broken up for building in later centuries, and prized for steps and kerbs; no source here gives an end to its use.

regions.text: Southern England: Salisbury Plain and the Marlborough Downs in Wiltshire, Kent, and less in Berkshire, Essex, Oxfordshire, Dorset and Hampshire

materials.technology: Too hard to dress, so used whole or broken with fire and later explosives; damp in buildings.

materials.name: York stone

period.text: Quarried in Yorkshire since the Middle Ages (1066 stands for them); East Riddlesden Hall was rebuilt of local Yorkshire stone in 1648. Still quarried, mostly for paving.

regions.text: Quarried around Leeds, Bradford, Halifax and Holmfirth in West Yorkshire; its paving all over Britain, London's traditional paving stone

materials.technology: Splits along its mica-rich layers into flags and roofing slates (thackstones); now often sawn.

materials.name: Reigate stone
